name: Sparsity-aware expert cache: request-level activation trace driving prefetch and eviction under host-RAM expert offload
arithmetic_intensity: The expert GEMM is unchanged. What changes is the byte term. With experts resident in host DRAM, a decode step moves k experts per layer over PCIe instead of reading all E experts from HBM, so the step is interconnect-bound at PCIe bandwidth rather than HBM-bound at the full expert footprint. Appendix B.2 says one I/O thread on pinned host memory plus DMA saturates PCIe 4.0, which they state as 32 GB/s, while the Table 1 caption says 24 GB/s for the same A5000 link. The two figures disagree and both are kept. A cache hit removes that transfer entirely. A wrong prefetch consumes the same bytes and additionally stalls the on-demand fetch behind it, which is why idle time, not GEMM time, dominates the Table 1 baselines. The predictor is a host-side cosine match: 21 us per query at 1K stored matrices and 226 us at 10K, against a token they time well above 120 ms, so the trace itself is not on the critical path.
scales_with: experts_per_token times expert_bytes, the PCIe payload per layer. Mixtral few large experts move more bytes per hit than Switch many small ones, and the paper own worst case is Mixtral at 836 ms

expert_cache_bytes left after the KV cache. DeepSeek-V2-Lite activates 3 GB per step; the buffer falls from above 3 GB below 32K context to 2 GB at 64K and 1 GB at 128K, after which the cache misses and on-demand fetch adds 137 ms
pcie_generation. One thread saturates PCIe 4.0; they add threads per GPU for newer PCIe
trace_warmup. The first iterations of a request have no request-level activation matrix, so prefetch cannot be scored and the first tokens pay full on-demand latency
batch_size. The skew the cache exploits is per request; pooled over 1000 sequences the reuse histogram flattens and the priority score stops distinguishing experts
workarounds: Pin expert buffers and issue the prefetch as async DMA from a dedicated I/O thread so the copy overlaps the current layer GEMM; one such thread is enough for PCIe 4.0
Score eviction by the matched request trace with an early-layer bias, not by LRU and not by next-index prefetch, since both evict the expert the next layer of this request needs
Keep the KV cache, attention and shared experts resident. Offloading the KV cache next to the experts makes the two streams contend, which is the long-context failure measured in vLLM
When the expert buffer drops below one step of activated bytes, stop prefetching and fall back to on-demand fetch rather than filling the link with predicted experts
Rebuild the trace per request. A collection of about 120 historical request matrices saturated latency across 290 tasks; matching more does not help and the cosine query grows from 21 us to 226 us
notes: Companion to papers/moe-infinity-sparsity-aware-expert-cache. The byte saving is a scheduling decision, not a kernel: a hand-written stack that already overlaps expert DMA with compute gets the win by changing which expert it fetches and which it evicts, using a request-scoped count matrix. It does not reduce bytes per expert, because the paper has no low-bit path, so it stacks with and does not replace a 2-4 bit expert GEMM. PCIe bandwidth is recorded as the authors stated it, 32 GB/s in Appendix B.2 and 24 GB/s in the Table 1 caption, without picking one. The 3.1-16.7x (abstract and Table 1) and 2.7-13.7x (Section 6) ranges are the authors claims against other offload systems, not against a fully resident GPU.
